newsitem.title: USA: Green issues attract voters to Democrats.
newsitem.headline: Green issues attract voters to Democrats.

text.p: The environment is proving to be a handy issue that candidates, especially Democrats, are using to court voters, and especially women, pollsters say.

Although "green" issues may not actually determine a voter's choice, candidates can be more or less attractive depending on their stance on environmental policies. "It's a powerful way to appeal to voters," said a Democratic national pollster, Celinda Lake.

Politicians -- mainly Democrats -- from President Bill Clinton on down have used pro-conservation stances to paint their opponents as old or out-of-touch and depict them as special-interest advocates who do not care about the public.
Negative advertisements featuring dead fish and grimy water have created images that strike a chord with voters even if they are not single-issue environmentalists.
One poll showed that 38 percent of voters considered the environment to be an important issue, with 50 percent of Democrats and 25 percent of Republicans rating it a major concern.

Taking advantage of those concerns, the League of Conservation Voters is running a $1.5 million campaign targeting 12 politicians for defeat in House and Senate races, including Republican Reps. Helen Chenoweth of Idaho, Michael Flanagan of Illinois and Frank Riggs of California, and Democratic Representative Gary Condit of California.

While the environment is considered a second-tier concern for voters, behind economic and moral issues, "it really plays big with swing voters," said Peter Snyder, senior project director for the Republican polling firm Luntz Research Companies.

Suburban mothers concerned about their children's future are fertile ground for environmental appeals, Snyder said. While most people were willing to pay a little money in taxes to help protect the environment, women were willing to spend more, according to Lake and Snyder.
Nevertheless, conservation had support among blue-collar men who favoured preserving forests, lakes and rivers for hunting and fishing.
The "hook and bullet crowd" also viewed development of environmental technology as a way for the United States to create jobs and stay ahead of its international competitors, Lake said.
The Democrats have been able to capitalise on Republicans' attempts to curb clean air and water regulations over the last two years by calling it a move to overturn protections.
"Republicans don't trust themselves on the environmental issue," Snyder said, adding that their economic rhetoric had killed their bid to make environmental laws more effective.
Contrasting attitudes toward environmental protection helped remind voters of the age gap between Clinton, 50, and Republican challenger Bob Dole, 73.
Lake quoted a poll respondent who was young enough to be Dole's grandchild, as saying: "We're the ones who taught our grandfathers about the environment."
While pollsters played up Republican vulnerability on the environmental front, Jerry Taylor of the libertarian think tank Cato Institute questioned the value of the polling data.
"This polling information is worthless," Taylor said. "It doesn't square with what we know people have done when actually forced to make a decision."
